theorem: Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space and let T: V -> V be linear. If T is injective, then T is surjective.
flawed_proof_steps: Thus im(T) = V, so T is surjective.
gold_diagnosis: The proof jumps from ker(T) = {0} to dim im(T) = dim V without citing rank-nullity or another valid dimension argument.
gold_minimal_repair: Insert the rank-nullity step: dim V = dim ker(T) + dim im(T), and since dim ker(T) = 0, dim im(T) = dim V.

theorem: Let G be a group and N a subgroup of G. If N is normal in G, then G/N is a group under coset multiplication.
assumptions: N is a subgroup of G
flawed_proof_steps: The elements of G/N are left cosets aN.
This operation is well-defined because N is a subgroup of G.
gold_diagnosis: Being a subgroup is not enough to make coset multiplication well-defined. Normality is the condition needed here.
gold_minimal_repair: Replace step 3 with: This operation is well-defined because N is normal in G.

theorem: Let phi: R -> S be a ring homomorphism. Then ker(phi) is an ideal of R.
assumptions: phi: R -> S is a ring homomorphism
flawed_proof_steps: Let a and b be in ker(phi). Then phi(a) = 0 and phi(b) = 0.
We have phi(a - b) = phi(a) - phi(b) = 0, so a - b is in ker(phi).
Thus ker(phi) is closed under subtraction.
Therefore ker(phi) is an ideal of R.
gold_diagnosis: The proof only shows additive subgroup closure. To prove ker(phi) is an ideal, it must also show absorption: for every r in R and a in ker(phi), both ra and ar are in ker(phi), depending on the ring convention.
gold_minimal_repair: Add the absorption step: for r in R and a in ker(phi), phi(ra) = phi(r)phi(a) = 0 and phi(ar) = phi(a)phi(r) = 0, so ra and ar are in ker(phi).
